title: What a sub-problem is
idea: MEET: a sub-problem is one small piece of a big problem that you already know how to solve on its own — splitting means naming those pieces.

options: A small piece of a big problem you can solve on its own
A bigger version of the problem
exercises.explanation: A sub-problem is a bite-sized piece — small enough that you already know a pattern for it.

exercises.prompt: Splitting a big problem means naming the smaller pieces it's made of.
exercises.explanation: Yes — decomposition is just listing the smaller, familiar jobs inside the big one.

exercises.prompt: PROBLEM: 'Show the total of the prices and how many are over 10.' One sub-problem is...
options: Add up the prices (a running total)
exercises.explanation: 'Add up the prices' is one small, familiar job — an accumulator. It's a sub-problem of the bigger task.

exercises.prompt: Why break a big problem into sub-problems?
options: Each small piece is something you already know how to solve
exercises.explanation: A big problem is scary; a list of small familiar jobs is not. Splitting turns one into the other.

exercises.prompt: Every sub-problem has to be something brand new you've never seen.
exercises.explanation: The opposite — a good sub-problem is something FAMILIAR: a total, a count, a biggest, a filter.

exercises.prompt: Select the pieces that could be sub-problems of 'average the passing scores'.
exercises.explanation: Filtering, totalling, and counting are all small familiar jobs. Together they build the average of the passers.

exercises.prompt: A big problem splits into THREE sub-problems. How many do you solve at a time?
options: One at a time — each on its own
exercises.explanation: Solve them one at a time. That's why we split — so each piece is simple and separate.

exercises.prompt: Match each big problem to one of its sub-problems.
exercises.explanation: Each big problem contains smaller familiar jobs. Naming one is the start of the split.

exercises.prompt: Order the idea: from big problem to sub-problems.
blocks: Notice the small familiar jobs inside it
Write each small job as a sub-problem
exercises.explanation: See the big problem, spot the familiar jobs, list them. That list is your decomposition.

options: A sub-problem is a small, familiar piece; splitting lists those pieces
A sub-problem is harder than the whole
exercises.explanation: Decomposition = naming the small familiar jobs inside a big problem. That's the whole unit.
